# What PSM I Changed About How I Think About Scrum

Before studying for Professional Scrum Master I, it was easy to see Scrum as a calendar: planning on Monday, stand-up every morning, review and retrospective at the end.

The deeper lesson was that the calendar is not the point. Scrum is a lightweight framework for addressing complex problems through empiricism.

## Events are places to make decisions

Transparency makes the current situation visible. Inspection looks at what that evidence means. Adaptation changes direction when the result is not acceptable.

The events create a regular rhythm for those three ideas:

- Sprint Planning establishes why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the work may be accomplished.
- The Daily Scrum inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the plan.
- The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and considers what to do next.
- The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.

Attendance without inspection or adaptation is only a meeting habit.

## Accountabilities are not job-title boxes

The Scrum Team contains one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and Developers. The team is self-managing and has no sub-teams or hierarchies inside it.

The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective Product Backlog management. Developers create a usable Increment each Sprint. The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and the Scrum Team’s effectiveness.

That is different from treating the Scrum Master as a task distributor or status collector.

## The Sprint Goal changed how I see scope

A Sprint is not successful merely because every planned task received a check mark. The Sprint Goal gives the work one objective and creates room to adapt the exact plan without losing purpose.

If the goal is “Counselors can reliably record and schedule lead follow-ups,” the team may change a technical approach or remove a low-value display detail while protecting the outcome. A flat task list makes all items look equally important.

## Done creates honesty

The Definition of Done makes the state of the Increment transparent. Work that does not meet it is not part of the Increment, however close it feels.

That principle is uncomfortable in a useful way. It prevents “90% done” work from being counted as usable product.

## Scrum is intentionally incomplete

The Scrum Guide does not prescribe estimation units, ticket formats, engineering practices, or project-management software. Teams can use helpful practices, but should not present those practices as mandatory parts of Scrum.

This changed the question I ask from “Are we following the ceremony?” to “Is this helping us inspect reality and adapt toward value?”

## What PSM I does not prove

Passing PSM I demonstrates foundational knowledge of the Scrum framework and how to apply it in situations assessed by Scrum.org. It does not equal employment as a Scrum Master, years of facilitation experience, or proof that I can handle every organizational challenge.

I present it as a foundation I continue to apply in requirements, work decomposition, review, and learning—not as borrowed seniority.

## Reference

[The official Scrum Guide, November 2020](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html)

> The most valuable change was simple: stop measuring Scrum by the number of meetings, and start looking for evidence of transparency, inspection, and adaptation.
